atomlings.title: Atomlings

how.hands: Hands: the bonds it makes (carbon 4, oxygen 2, hydrogen 1). Metals hold out the electrons they give away.
how.hoop: The hoop: its outer electrons, set out like Lewis dots; a hollow ring is a place still free.
how.size: Size: its real atomic radius (big at the bottom left of the table, small at the top right).
how.move: Gases float (the lighter than air, the higher), liquids slide, solids walk.
how.body: Metals shine like metal; non-metals are see-through, with the nucleus inside; metalloids are half and half.
how.mark: On its head, its family: a flame, a helmet, spikes, a halo…
how.look: Colours: a metal wears its own colour, a flame burns in its flame-test colour, and each column of metals shares a helmet shape.
how.story: Objects: most carry something from their own story, like helium's balloon, chlorine's swim ring, gold's crown or thorium's hammer. Tap one to find out why.

atomlings.tap: Tap an Atomling to read it.

about.title: About Element Worlds
about.what: A periodic table you can walk into. Every element is a cube on the plaza; inside, each cube is bigger than it looks: a hall about that element, and for some elements whole worlds to explore. Made for curious people of ten and of every other age.

how.table: On the plaza: drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom, click a cube for its card, click it again (or press Enter) to go in. Arrow keys walk from cube to cube.
how.inside: Inside: walk up to a panel or an exhibit and press E (or tap the button) to read or use it. Every one you read is a discovery.
how.views: Two ways to walk: as the element's own Atomling, or in first person. V switches between them.
how.levels: Explorer tells it simply; Scientist adds the numbers, the units and the why. Switch at the top.
how.time: The time machine shows the table growing through history, from the elements known since ancient times to the last ones made in laboratories.

about.data: Element data from the PubChem periodic table (US National Library of Medicine, public domain) and the mendeleev Python package (MIT licence): masses, configurations, radii, isotopes, abundances. Discovery years follow one rule (when the element was first recognised or isolated). Values for the superheavy elements are partly predictions and are marked as such.
about.privacy: To make the game better we note what is visited and done here (which halls, for how long, what was tried in the lab), never names or addresses. When you are signed in it is kept with your account; otherwise each visit is anonymous, and nothing is noted when your browser asks not to be tracked. You can switch it off under 👤.
about.recording: You are signed in as “{{who}}”: what you play is kept with your account.

lab.ionic: Ionic: the metal handed its electrons over and the ions hold on by attraction. In a real crystal there are no molecules: every ion sits among ions of the other charge.
lab.metals: Two metals do not hold hands: in a metal, electrons wander among all the atoms. Join a metal to a non-metal instead.
lab.title: Molecule Lab
lab.start: Pick an atom on the left. Tap two atoms to join their hands; tap a bond to let go.
lab.stable: Every hand is held: a stable molecule!
lab.help: Tap an atom, then another, to join hands. Tap the same pair again for a double bond. Drag to turn, scroll to zoom.

forge.title: Atom Forge
forge.commonestTip: The neutrons of this element's commonest isotope
forge.holdTip: A force field holds the nucleus together while you build
forge.chartKid: Every kind of nucleus ever seen: protons going up, neutrons going across. White ones last for ever; the others break apart, red ones slowly, blue ones in a flash. Tap one to build it.
forge.chartSci: All 3552 known nuclides (NUBASE, via the mendeleev package): Z up, N across, coloured by half-life. The white band is the valley of stability; it bends toward N > Z as the protons' repulsion grows. Tap to build.
